name: Epigenetic Aging Clocks
title: Epigenetic Aging Clocks
answer: Epigenetic aging clocks are models that estimate biological age from DNA methylation patterns at specific CpG sites, often differing from chronological age. They are used in genomic medicine and precision therapeutics to measure aging, assess intervention effects, and stratify patients in clinical research. The field includes first-generation clocks trained on chronological age and second-generation clocks trained on morbidity or mortality outcomes. This site tracks these models within its broader catalog of medical AI models and scientific models.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Epigenetic aging clocks are models that estimate biological age from DNA methylation patterns at specific CpG sites, often differing from chronological age. They are used in genomic medicine and precision therapeutics to measure aging, assess intervention effects, and stratify patients in clinical research. The field includes first-generation clocks trained on chronological age and second-generation clocks trained on morbidity or mortality outcomes. This site tracks these models within its broader catalog of medical AI models and scientific models.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The clocks run on standard genomic data infrastructure, including DNA methylation arrays such as the Illumina 450K and EPIC platforms, or bisulfite sequencing data. Computation is modest, typically a linear or regularized regression over a few hundred CpG sites, so it can run on a laptop or a clinical bioinformatics server. No specialized accelerator hardware is required, and the main bottleneck is sample processing and quality control of methylation data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by training penalized regression models, often elastic net, on methylation beta values from large cohorts with known ages or health outcomes. A clock outputs an age estimate, and the difference between that estimate and chronological age is called age acceleration. Researchers validate clocks in longitudinal cohorts and use them as surrogate endpoints in trials of interventions that may affect aging. The models are interpretable at the level of CpG site weights, though the biological meaning of individual sites is often unclear.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on data provenance, consent, and the potential for age estimates to be used in insurance, employment, or forensic settings. Methylation data is sensitive personal health information, and clocks trained on one population may perform poorly on another, creating fairness and validity concerns. Product liability questions are relevant if a clock is sold as a diagnostic or wellness tool and its output causes harm, and this site tracks active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies as well as compliance and regulation pages. No clock should be treated as a definitive measure of individual health without clinical validation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going is toward multi-omic clocks that combine methylation with proteomics, transcriptomics, and clinical labs to improve accuracy and mechanistic insight. There is also movement toward single-cell and tissue-specific clocks, and toward using clocks as primary endpoints in human longevity trials. As regulatory frameworks for AI diagnostics mature, epigenetic clocks may move from research tools to regulated clinical decision support, with clearer standards for validation and reporting.
